subject: Questions regarding the monte Carlo approach for model evaluation

messages.author: 9e019d17a5eaef1a
messages.subject: Questions regarding the monte Carlo approach for model evaluation
parts:
Hello everyone! 


I am currently trying to fit a model with 46 items, however, I have only 150 participants per group (3 groups). When fitting the model to the separate groups, the CFI value was not acceptable <.90. I'd like to know if it was due to insufficient sample size. I was suggested to run a simulation study. 

I found the simsem package, which in Example 7 (analyzing real data and then run monte carlo simulation https://github.com/simsem/simsem/wiki/Example-7:-Analyzing-Real-Data-and-then-Run-Monte-Carlo-Simulation), it said, "As a benefit, this procedure will yield a distribution of fit indices from simulated data when the hypothesized model is correct. This distribution can compare with the result of the real data. This procedure is called a Monte Carlo approach for model evaluation."

I have a few questions about it:
1) does it mean that if the fit indices from the real sample (e.g. CFI) is greater than the alpha = 0.05 cufoff value from the the simulations, then the hypothesized model can be accepted?
2) can I do the simulations with a bigger sample size than the original n? For example, the fit indices distribution with n=500 per group? Does it make sense?
3) Is there any emperical or methodological literature regarding this approach? From reading the threads, I was directed to a paper by Preacher and Selig (2012) which, if I understood correctly, advocated the monte carlo approach to evaluate indirect effects confidence intervals. Is that the same thing as evaluating model fits?
4) are there any guidelines in terms of the allowed misspecifications in the simulations? e.g., the crossloadings specified in the example were between -0.2 and 0.2.
5) The above questions are all about fitting the hypothesized model to a single group, will this approach also work for multiple-group invariance testing? Is there also a need to specify misspecifications for the multiple group simulations? 

I am just recently looking at simulations/bootstrap in sem. I sincerely apologize if these questions seem too naive. Thank you very much in advance!

Erin

messages.author: ad188126f9138663
messages.subject: Re: Questions regarding the monte Carlo approach for model evaluation
parts:
Erin,
  I am not a statistician but here is my take on your questions.
1) does it mean that if the fit indices from the real sample (e.g. CFI) is greater than the alpha = 0.05 cufoff value from the the simulations, then the hypothesized model can be accepted?

As in any other situation, decisions about fit and model acceptance should never be made on the basis of one number, not even compared to a reference distribution.  Consider a variety of indices, do not ignore chi-square, and also look at local fit information such as estimates and residuals.  If your CFI is in the rejection region, it means that it is unlikely to have been generated if the model were correct.  If the CFI falls outside the rejection region, between the tails, then you cannot rule out your model, but the same could likely be said for many rival hypotheses as well.
2) can I do the simulations with a bigger sample size than the original n? For example, the fit indices distribution with n=500 per group? Does it make sense?
This will tell you what you would expect if you ran the study with more cases and the model used to simulate the data were correct.

3) Is there any emperical or methodological literature regarding this approach? From reading the threads, I was directed to a paper by Preacher and Selig (2012) which, if I understood correctly, advocated the monte carlo approach to evaluate indirect effects confidence intervals. Is that the same thing as evaluating model fits?
They are analogous, allowing for the fact that the tests are reversed.  For a parameter, the null hypothesis is zero.  For fit, the analog to a null hypothesis is perfect fit.
4) are there any guidelines in terms of the allowed misspecifications in the simulations? e.g., the crossloadings specified in the example were between -0.2 and 0.2.

The simulation assumes that the simulated model is correctly specified.  You can explore the impact of misspecification with further simulations (e.g., with corss-loadings) but these results are specific to the pattern of misspecification that you simulate.

5) The above questions are all about fitting the hypothesized model to a single group, will this approach also work for multiple-group invariance testing? Is there also a need to specify misspecifications for the multiple group simulations?

I do not see anything that would prevent you from trying this.  However, there is no magic here.  The more complex the model, the more you are pressing the limits of your data.  My guess is that your simulations will confirm that it is very hard to answer your questions based on your data.  You might explore using a Bayesian approach to compensate for lack of data by making stronger explicit assumptions.  However, there is really no getting around the limited size of your data set except by collecting more data.  The Bayesian approach would just give you more flexibility in the balance that you choose between  paying for the small sample in the currency of low power and in the currency of strong assumptions.

Keith
